According to Mark Gurman's latest "Power On" newsletter, Apple is reportedly considering multiple changes to its App Store. The goal? To boost the potential revenue the App Store brings in.

Apple's reform plans for the App Store are not yet clear. Bloomberg's Mark Gurman reports that Apple wants to "find ways to improve profit margins and extract more recurring revenue from the platform," with the work primarily driven by incoming CEO John Ternus and current Senior Vice President of Services Eddy Cue.

Reportedly, this overhaul was one of the reasons senior employee Phil Schiller left Apple last week. Schiller stepped down as Senior Vice President of Marketing in 2020 to become an Apple Fellow, at which time part of his responsibilities included overseeing the App Store. Schiller was not in favor of the related ideas:

Apple has many ways it could improve the App Store's profit margins. For example, it could eliminate its manual app review process—an expensive and questionable procedure in the age of automated coding. Further automating review would likely anger users, but would undoubtedly save costs.

Apple could also raise developer membership fees, currently $99 per year. Given that many small developers spend $200 a month subscribing to Codex and Claude to build apps, Apple is well-positioned to raise prices without much pushback. The company could also charge large developers subscription fees based on traffic, passing on some of its infrastructure costs.

The final result remains to be seen, but I'm very much looking forward to seeing what these changes ultimately look like.
